The Levant was a busy corridor around a million years ago. Long before it became a place where modern humans and Neanderthals mingled, the narrow land bridge linking Africa to Eurasia proved to be a popular thoroughfare for other ancient hominins who settled in the region (most likely Homo erectus and Homo heidelbergensis). Unfortunately, there’s still a lot we don’t know about the paleoclimate there, but we recently got some clues thanks to an elephant’s tooth.

The tooth, dated to around 700,000 years ago, was discovered alongside tusk fragments and a cache of basalt hand axes from the same period in the Daughters of Jacob Bridge region just south of Israel’s Hula Valley. A research team led by archaeologists from Haifa University performed some high-tech dentistry on the tooth, employing CT scans, 3D construction, and isotopic analysis, and recently published their results in Quaternary Science Reviews.  

Read more: “Here’s What the Whiskers on an Elephant’s Trunk Do”

According to their analysis, the tooth belongs to the extinct straight-tusked pachyderm Palaeoloxodon antiquus—one of the largest mammals to ever live (and much bigger than modern elephants). While that’s impressive in its own right, it also contains a kind of bioarchive of what the prehistoric Levant was like when these mysterious hominins left their hand axes behind.

The carbon isotopes within the tooth indicate its owner lived in an environment where water was plentiful. Patterns of microwear show the elephant fed on vegetation commonly found in woodlands and river environments. Pollen grains found surrounding the tooth originated from aquatic plants, reeds, and willows. Taken together, the analyses paint a picture of a lush landscape of woodlands and marshes—an idyllic place for ancient hominins and elephants alike.

“The availability of water, vegetation, and animal resources shaped where humans and wildlife could survive,” study author Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona explained in a statement. “The wetlands, rivers, and woodlands of the Hula Valley helped sustain life along one of the world's earliest migration corridors, offering a rare opportunity to understand the ecological conditions that supported both animals and human populations nearly 700,000 years ago.”
